title: Binary tree problems: views, levels, diameter, same tree
overview: This module is a problem-solving practice round on binary trees. Almost every solution is one of two tools: a **recursive DFS** that asks the left and right subtrees and combines their answers, or a **BFS with a queue of (node, level) pairs** that knows which level each node is on. Once you can pick the right tool, problems like left/right view, node level, diameter and same-tree become short.

concepts.explain: Solve the problem for `root->left` and `root->right`, then combine the two answers at the root. The base case is almost always `root == NULL`.
Push `{node, level}` pairs into the queue. When you pop a node you know its level, and its children get `level + 1`.

concepts.term: First node seen on a level
concepts.explain: In BFS, the first node you pop on each level is the leftmost one (if you push left before right). Mark levels you have already seen with a `bool` array to keep only that first node. Push right first and you get the right view instead.

concepts.term: Diameter = best left height + right height
concepts.explain: The longest path through a node goes down its left side and down its right side. Compute heights recursively and, at every node, update a global maximum with `l + r`.

Two trees are the same if both are empty, or both roots have the same value and their left subtrees match and their right subtrees match. A shape difference (one is NULL, the other not) means different.
A DFS that visits left before right collects leaves from left to right. Two trees are leaf-similar when those lists are equal.
`pair<A, B>` holds two values, read with `.first` and `.second`. It is what lets a queue store a node together with its level.

files.title: STL pair basics
files.what: Shows the ways to create a `pair` (`make_pair` and braces), a pair of `string` and `int`, and a `vector` of pairs, then tries to read `n` pairs from input.
steps: `p1 = make_pair(2, 3)` builds a pair; `.first` is 2 and `.second` is 3.
`p2 = {2, 3}` does the same with brace syntax, which is shorter.
`p3` shows the two parts can have different types: `pair<string, int>`.
A `vector<pair<int,int>>` gets two pairs with `push_back` and is printed with a loop.
Finally it reads `n` and wants to fill a vector of `n` pairs with `cin >> v[i].first >> v[i].second`.
files.input_note: n, then n lines of two integers (the program never gets this far because it does not compile).
files.output_note: You will see a compile error instead of output: the name `v` is declared twice in `main`.
files.watch_out: `vector<pair<int, int>> v(n);` redeclares `v`, which already exists above, so the file does not compile. Fix: give the second vector another name, e.g. `vector<pair<int,int>> v2(n);`, and use `v2` in the input loop.

check.q: How do you read the second value of a pair `p`?

files.title: Is node present? (early return)
files.what: Checks whether the value `x` exists anywhere in the tree using a recursive DFS that stops as soon as it finds it.
steps: If `root` is NULL there is nothing here, so return `false`.
If `root->data == x`, we found it: return `true`.
Search the left subtree; if it says `true`, return `true` right away without touching the right side.
Otherwise search the right subtree and return `true` if found.
If neither side has it, return `false`.
files.input_note: Tree in level order (-1 = no child): 1 with children 2, 3; 2 with children 4, 5. Then the values to look for, one per line: 5 and 7.
files.output_note: One line per query: `isNodePresent(5) = true` because 5 is a child of 2, and `isNodePresent(7) = false` because no node holds 7.

check.q: Why check the left result before calling the right side?
check.a: If the value is already found on the left, there is no need to search the right subtree, which saves work.

files.title: Is node present? (return left || right)
files.what: Same search, but it always calls both sides and returns `left || right`. Shorter to write, but it searches the right subtree even when the left one already found `x`.
steps: Same base cases: NULL gives `false`, a matching value gives `true`.
Call both `isNodePresent(root->left, x)` and `isNodePresent(root->right, x)`.
Return `left || right`.
files.input_note: Tree in level order (-1 = no child): 1 with children 2, 3; 2 with children 4, 5. Then the values to look for, one per line: 5 and 7.
files.output_note: Same answers as version 1: `isNodePresent(5) = true` and `isNodePresent(7) = false`. Only the amount of work differs, not the result.

check.q: How could you make version 2 stop early and still stay one line?
check.a: `return isNodePresent(root->left, x) || isNodePresent(root->right, x);` — `||` skips the right call when the left is true.

files.title: Node level with BFS
files.what: Finds on which level (root = 1) a given value sits, using BFS where each queue item carries its level.
steps: Empty tree: return 0.
Push `{root, 1}` into a queue of `pair<TreeNode<int>*, int>`.
Pop the front, split it into `node` and `level`.
If `node->val == value`, return `level` right away.
Otherwise push the existing children with `level + 1`.
If the queue empties without a match, return 0.
files.input_note: Tree in level order (1; 2 3; 4 5 under 2), then the values to find, one per line: 1, 5 and 9.
files.output_note: `nodeLevel(1) = 1` (the root), `nodeLevel(5) = 3` (5 is under 2, which is under 1), and `nodeLevel(9) = 0` because 9 is not in the tree.

check.q: What level does a child get?

files.title: Left view of a binary tree

problem.name: Code360 - Left View Of a Binary Tree

files.what: Meant to print the first node of each level as seen from the left. The file actually contains the LeetCode **right** side view code (same as `leetcode_binary_tree_right_side_view.cpp`).
steps: BFS with `{node, level}` pairs, starting at level 1.
A `bool freq[105]` array remembers which levels already gave an answer.
The first node popped on a new level is added to `ans` and the level is marked.
Children are pushed **right first, then left**, so the first node on each level is the rightmost one.
files.input_note: The tree [1,2,3,null,5,null,4] in level order: 1; 2 3; 2 has only a right child 5; 3 has only a right child 4. The file has only `rightSideView`, so the driver calls that.
files.output_note: Prints `[1,3,4]`, which is the **right** view. The real left view of this tree is `[1,2,5]`, so this file gives the wrong answer for the left-view problem.
files.watch_out: This is the right-view code pasted into the left-view file (LeetCode's `Solution`/`TreeNode` shape, not Code360's function). For the left view, push `node->left` before `node->right` and use Code360's function name and node type. Also `freq[105]` only works if the tree has at most 104 levels.

check.q: Which single change turns a right-view BFS into a left-view BFS?
check.a: Push the left child before the right child, so the leftmost node on each level is popped first.

files.title: Binary tree right side view

problem.name: LeetCode 199 - Binary Tree Right Side View

files.what: Returns the values you would see standing on the right of the tree: the rightmost node of each level. BFS pushes the right child first, so the first node met on a level is the rightmost.
steps: If `root` exists, push `{root, 1}`.
Pop a pair; `node = parent.first`, `level = parent.second`.
If `freq[level]` is still false, this is the first node of that level: add `node->val` and set `freq[level] = true`.
Push `node->right` then `node->left`, each with `level + 1`.
Return `ans` when the queue is empty.
files.input_note: LeetCode example 1, [1,2,3,null,5,null,4], in level order with -1 for missing children.
files.output_note: Prints `rightSideView = [1,3,4]`, the same as LeetCode's expected answer: 1 on level 1, 3 on level 2, 4 on level 3 (5 is hidden behind 4).
files.watch_out: LeetCode allows up to 100 nodes, so `freq[105]` is enough there; for bigger trees use a `vector<bool>` or compare `level` with `ans.size()` instead.

check.a: Several nodes share a level; the array makes sure only the first one popped on each level is recorded.

files.title: Reverse level order traversal
files.what: Does a normal level order traversal into a vector and then reverses the whole vector.
steps: Push the root (if any) into a queue.
Pop a node, append its `val` to `v`, push its left then right child.
After the loop, `reverse(v.begin(), v.end())`.
Return `v`.
files.input_note: Tree in level order: 1; 2 3; 4 5 under 2; then -1 pairs for the leaves.
files.output_note: Prints `[5,4,3,2,1]`: normal level order is 1 2 3 4 5, and the whole list is reversed.
files.watch_out: Reversing the whole list also reverses the order inside each level (right to left). That is exactly what this Code360 problem expects; some other versions want each level left to right, which needs pushing right child first before reversing.

check.q: What does this function return for a tree with only the root 7?

files.title: Special (full) binary tree check
files.what: A tree is special when every node has either 0 or 2 children. The function checks each node recursively.
steps: An empty tree counts as special: return `true`.
If exactly one child is missing (left NULL but right present, or the other way), return `false`.
Otherwise check both subtrees recursively.
Return `l && r`: all nodes must pass.
files.input_note: First the number of trees (2), then each tree in level order. Tree 1: 1; 2 3; 4 5 under 2. Tree 2: 1; 2 3; only a left child 4 under 2.
files.output_note: One line per tree: `true` for the first (every node has 0 or 2 children) and `false` for the second (node 2 has only one child).

check.q: Is a single leaf node a special binary tree?

files.title: Diameter of a binary tree (Code360)
files.what: The diameter is the number of edges on the longest path between two nodes. While computing heights, each node checks the path that bends through it: left height + right height.
steps: `mx` is a global that holds the best diameter so far; set it to 0 first.
`max_height` returns 0 for NULL and 1 for a leaf (height counted in nodes).
For other nodes it gets `l` and `r`, the heights of both subtrees.
`d = l + r` is the number of edges on the longest path through this node; update `mx`.
Return `max(l, r) + 1` so the parent gets this node's height.
`diameterOfBinaryTree` calls it once and returns `mx`.
files.output_note: Prints `diameter = 3`: the longest path is 4-2-1-3 (or 5-2-1-3), which has 3 edges.
files.watch_out: The longest path does not have to pass through the root, which is why `mx` is updated at every node, not only at the root.

check.q: Why do we need a global (or reference) `mx` instead of just returning the height?
check.a: The function returns height to its parent, but the best diameter might be found deep inside the tree, so it has to be stored somewhere separate.

files.title: Diameter of a binary tree (LeetCode)
files.what: The same algorithm inside LeetCode's `Solution` class; `mx` becomes a member variable instead of a global.
steps: Reset `mx = 0`, call `max_height(root)`.
At each node, update `mx` with `l + r` and return `max(l, r) + 1`.
Return `mx`.
files.input_note: LeetCode example 1, [1,2,3,4,5], in level order with -1 for missing children.
files.output_note: Prints `diameterOfBinaryTree = 3`, matching LeetCode's expected output for `[1,2,3,4,5]`.

check.q: What is the diameter of a tree with only one node?

files.title: Root equals sum of children

problem.name: LeetCode 2236 - Root Equals Sum of Children

files.what: The tree always has exactly three nodes, so the answer is just one comparison.
steps: Read `root->left->val` and `root->right->val`.
Return whether their sum equals `root->val`.
files.input_note: Number of trees, then each three-node tree in level order: the LeetCode examples [10,4,6] and [5,3,1].
files.output_note: `checkTree = true` for [10,4,6] (4 + 6 = 10) and `checkTree = false` for [5,3,1] (3 + 1 is 4, not 5), as in LeetCode's examples.
files.watch_out: This only works because the problem guarantees both children exist; on a general tree `root->left` could be NULL and crash.

check.q: Why is no recursion needed here?
check.a: The tree is guaranteed to be exactly a root with two children.

files.title: Univalued binary tree
files.what: Checks that every node has the same value as the root by passing the root's value down a recursive helper.
steps: `isUnivalTree` takes `root->val` as the target value.
`isUnivalHelper` returns true for NULL.
If a node's value differs from `value`, return false.
Otherwise both subtrees must also be univalued: `left && right`.
files.input_note: Number of trees, then the LeetCode examples [1,1,1,1,1,null,1] and [2,2,2,5,2] in level order.
files.output_note: `true` for the all-ones tree and `false` for the second tree because of the 5, matching LeetCode's examples.

check.q: Why pass `value` down instead of comparing each node with its parent?
check.a: Either works; passing the root's value keeps one fixed target and makes the check a single comparison per node.

files.title: Leaf-similar trees
files.what: Collects the leaves of each tree from left to right into two vectors and compares the vectors.
steps: `leafSequence` does a DFS: NULL returns, a leaf is pushed into `leaves`.
For inner nodes it visits left first, then right, so leaves come out left to right.
Build `leaves1` and `leaves2` for the two roots.
Return `leaves1 == leaves2` (vector `==` compares size and every element).
files.complexity: Time O(n1 + n2) · Space O(n1 + n2)
files.input_note: LeetCode example 1: root1 = [3,5,1,6,2,9,8,null,null,7,4] and root2 = [3,5,1,6,7,4,2,null,null,null,null,null,null,9,8], one tree per line in level order.
files.output_note: Prints `leafSimilar = true`, as LeetCode expects: both trees have the leaf sequence 6 7 4 9 8 even though their shapes differ.
files.watch_out: The vector is passed by reference (`vector<int>&`); without the `&` each call would fill its own copy and the result would stay empty.

check.q: Why must the DFS visit the left child before the right?
check.a: So the leaves are collected in left-to-right order, which is the order the problem compares.

files.title: Same tree (empty placeholder)
files.what: Only a comment with the problem link; the actual solutions are in the version1 and version2 files.
steps: The file holds just the link to the problem.
See `leetcode_same_tree_version1.cpp` (compare traversals) and `leetcode_same_tree_version2.cpp` (compare recursively).
files.output_note: This file holds only the problem link, so there is nothing to test and no harness. Building it fails with a linker error about a missing `main` (`WinMain`). The real solutions are in version1 and version2.
files.watch_out: This file only holds the problem link, not code, so it cannot be built on its own (the linker error above just means there is no `main`). Open the version1 and version2 files for the solutions.

check.q: What two things must match for two trees to be the same?
check.a: Their shape and the value at every position.

files.title: Same tree by comparing traversals
files.what: Writes each tree as a preorder list, recording a special marker `-1001` for every missing child, then compares the two lists.
steps: The helper (named `inorder`, but it is really **preorder**) pushes `node->val`, then goes left, then right.
When it reaches NULL it pushes `-1001`, meant as a value that never appears in the tree (see Watch out).
Both trees are turned into `result1` and `result2`.
The trees are the same exactly when the lists are equal.
files.input_note: Number of test pairs (3), then two trees per pair in level order: the LeetCode examples [1,2,3] vs [1,2,3], [1,2] vs [1,null,2], and [1,2,1] vs [1,1,2].
files.output_note: Three lines, matching LeetCode's examples: `true` (identical trees), `false` ([1,2] gives `1 2 X X X` but [1,null,2] gives `1 X 2 X X`), `false` (values in different places).
files.watch_out: The NULL markers are what make this correct: without them `[1,2]` and `[1,null,2]` would both give `1 2`. The marker must be a value that can never be a node value; LeetCode 100 limits values to -10^4..10^4, so `-1001` could clash with a real node. A safer marker is something like `INT_MIN`.

check.q: Why does a plain preorder list (without NULL markers) fail to identify a tree?
check.a: Different shapes can give the same order of values, e.g. a left child vs. a right child.

files.title: Same tree by direct recursion
files.what: The cleaner solution: compare the two roots, then compare left with left and right with right.
steps: Both NULL: same, return true.
Only one NULL: shapes differ, return false.
Otherwise return `p->val == q->val && isSameTree(p->left, q->left) && isSameTree(p->right, q->right)`.
`&&` stops at the first mismatch, so it does not waste work.
files.input_note: Number of test pairs (3), then two trees per pair in level order: the LeetCode examples [1,2,3] vs [1,2,3], [1,2] vs [1,null,2], and [1,2,1] vs [1,1,2].
files.watch_out: Keep the order of the base cases: check "both NULL" before "one NULL", otherwise two empty trees would be reported as different.

check.q: Which is better, version 1 or version 2, and why?
check.a: Version 2: no extra lists (O(h) memory), no marker value to choose, and it stops at the first difference.

practice_links.name: Left View Of a Binary Tree

recap: Most tree problems are either "ask both subtrees and combine" (DFS) or "walk level by level" (BFS).
Store `{node, level}` pairs in the queue whenever the answer depends on the level.
Left view = first node per level with left pushed first; right view = push right first.
Diameter: update a global best with `left height + right height` at every node.
Two trees are equal when both are NULL, or values match and both pairs of subtrees match.
Judge solutions have no `main`; to test locally, add a node class, a tree builder and a `main`.

check_yourself.q: For the tree 1 (2, 3) where 2 has a right child 4, what are the left view and the right view?
Why can't the diameter simply be height(left) + height(right) of the root?
check_yourself.a: The longest path may lie entirely inside one subtree and never touch the root.

check_yourself.q: In a BFS, if a node is on level 3, which level are its children on?
When does `p == NULL || q == NULL` mean the trees differ?
check_yourself.a: When it is reached after ruling out both being NULL: exactly one tree has a node there, so the shapes differ.
